scenes.headline: How a detector shows its work
scenes.sub: A sum of named features, not a score
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Rook! Most AI text detectors give you a score and no reason. Here is how a sparse autoencoder turns one into a sum you can read.

scenes.text: Put a sparse autoencoder under the verdict. Keep only features that have a validated description, then let a linear model add them up.
scenes.mark: a linear model add them up
scenes.say: Put a sparse autoencoder under the verdict. Keep only the features with a validated description, then let a plain linear model add them up.

scenes.title: From activations to an auditable verdict

steps.say: Run the text through the language model and read its residual stream at several depths.
A sparse autoencoder rewrites each activation as a few active features.
Take each feature's largest value across the document.
Mask out features without a validated description. The linear head weighs the rest.

scenes.text: logit = sum of w x activation + bias
scenes.title: Why the sum is exact

parts.say: Each term is a weight times one feature's activation, which is that feature's exact effect on the verdict.
Add the bias and nothing is left over.

scenes.say: Because the head is linear, the verdict is a plain sum.

scenes.label: AUC in the toy's training domains
scenes.say: In my toy rebuild, the detector reached zero point nine nine five AUC in its training domains.

scenes.label: human documents flagged in wiki_csai
scenes.say: Yet on human encyclopedia text from another domain, it flagged eighty-one in a hundred. The audit showed why.

scenes.text: A verdict made of named parts can be argued with. Test it on the texts and the writers it will actually judge.
scenes.say: A verdict made of named parts can be argued with. Still test it on the texts and writers it will judge.
